# Reading the thread — the tells that tell you where the power actually sits

Most of what you need is already in the message they sent you. People leak their constraints
constantly, and almost nobody reads for it.

## Tells about their budget

| What they wrote | What it usually means |
|---|---|
| Names a number unprompted | It is not their ceiling. There is room above it, usually 20–40% |
| "What are your rates?" with no budget named | They have a number and are hoping yours is lower |
| "We have a limited budget for this one" | There is a bigger budget for something else. Ask what that is |
| "This is more of a partnership than a paid thing" | No budget line exists, and they need you to solve that internally |
| A number arrives with a deliverable quietly added | The number was set before the scope. Reprice the scope, not the number |
| "Can you do it for exposure / product" | Their alternative to you is genuinely weak, or they think yours is |

## Tells about their timeline

**A deadline they mention twice is real.** A deadline mentioned once, in passing, is aspirational.

**"When could you start?" before terms are agreed** means they have already told someone
internally this is happening. That is the strongest signal in the whole thread — their reputation
is now attached to it landing.

**Silence after enthusiasm is almost never disinterest.** It is an internal blocker: a budget
that has not been approved, a boss who said no, a reorganisation. Ask a diagnostic question
rather than applying pressure. "Is this still moving on your side, or has something shifted?"
gets a real answer far more often than a chase does.

## Tells about who actually decides

- **"I'll need to check with the team"** — they do not sign. Find out who does, and what that
  person is optimising for. It is rarely the same thing.
- **A new name appears on the thread** — the decision moved up. Everything already agreed is now
  reopened, whether or not anyone says so.
- **They cc someone and that person never speaks** — that is the approver, reading.
- **An agency between you and the brand** — the agency's margin is not your problem, and the
  brand usually does not know the agency is grinding you. That gap is leverage, used carefully.

## Tells about how much they have already spent

This is the row people forget, and it is often decisive. Every one of these raises the cost of
them walking away:

- They have had internal meetings about it
- They named you specifically rather than "a creator in this space"
- They have a launch date the work is attached to
- They have already sent a contract, a brief or a deck
- They have told a client, a boss or a public audience it is happening

**The more of these are true, the more expensive your no becomes for them** — and the less
plausible it is that they walk over a reasonable counter.

## The question that resolves most stalls

When a thread has gone quiet and you cannot tell why, this outperforms a chase:

> "Is this still live on your side? Happy either way, I just want to know whether to hold the
> slot."

It is warm, it names a real constraint, it gives them permission to say no — and a no is worth
more than a maybe you keep paying attention to.

## What NOT to read as a tell

- **A slow reply is not disinterest.** People are busy and inboxes are bad.
- **A short reply is not coldness.** Some people write short.
- **Enthusiasm is not commitment.** "This looks amazing!" costs nothing to type. Look for a date,
  a number or a name — those cost something.
